section_summary: This section documents the severe regulatory and financial pressures confronting American motion picture distributors in Japan following the enactment of the 1939 Motion Picture Law. The documents trace diplomatic negotiations between the Department of State, the American Embassy in Tokyo, and industry representatives over draconian film import quotas, blocked revenues nearing five million yen, and bans on foreign newsreels. A major controversy emerges when National City Bank demanded the withdrawal of millions of yen in distributor deposits, prompting Paramount to invest blocked yen into Japanese national bonds against State Department objections.

subfiles.about: Home Office regulations detailing censorship criteria, certificate issuance, licensing, and exhibition limits under the Motion Picture Law.
subfiles.summary: These articles define prohibited film themes, censorship seal procedures, inspection fee rates, and mandatory screening of cultural films. Dramatic foreign films are restricted to fifty prints per theatre per year, and screenings are limited to three hours per session. Safety switch requirements, projectionist licensing, and restrictions on minor admissions are also codified.
subfiles.title: Home Office Ordinance for the Enforcement of the Motion Picture Law (Articles 28-58 and Additional Provisions)

subfiles.about: Imperial ordinance specifying production and distribution businesses and ministerial responsibilities under the Motion Picture Law.
subfiles.summary: Promulgated on September 26, 1939, this ordinance defines commercial motion picture production and distribution enterprises. It also apportions regulatory jurisdiction over various articles of the Motion Picture Law between the Minister of Home Affairs and the Minister of Education.
subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 668: Motion Picture Law Enforcement Ordinance

subfiles.about: Discussion of Japanese import quotas on American motion pictures and the questionable role of intermediary Hisaji Kubo.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (J. M. Jones)
subfiles.summary: Colonel F. L. Herron called on the State Department to urge diplomatic action against Japan's severe quota of 120 foreign films, which threatened to expel American distributors. Herron disclosed that intermediary Hisaji Kubo was untrustworthy and that distributors had ceased dealings with him. State Department officers advised submitting factual evidence of financial harm so Ambassador Grew could make informal representations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Restrictions in Japan upon the Importation of American Films and upon Exchange Remittances

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Tokyo cable on 1940 film import allocations and request for a vigorous diplomatic protest.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Herron writes to Raymond C. Mackay requesting a strong protest by the Tokyo Embassy against new decrees limiting foreign films to 120 per year. He attaches a December 23 cable from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan detailing company quotas and 5,000,000 yen in accumulated blocked funds. The cable recommends against outright sales to Japanese distributors and urges inclusion of the film problem in broader trade treaty discussions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Raymond C. Mackay Transmitting Tokyo Cable

subfiles.about: Transmittal to Ambassador Grew of conference memorandum and industry correspondence concerning film restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo confidential copies of the January 3 memorandum of conversation with Colonel Herron and Herron's letter of January 10. The instruction references telegram No. 20 regarding restrictions on American films and exchange remittances in Japan.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1887 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo

subfiles.about: Departmental note recording telephone advice to Colonel Herron regarding instructions sent to Ambassador Grew.
subfiles.summary: This internal memorandum notes that Colonel Herron was informed by telephone on January 16 that an instruction had been sent to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo. It concludes that no further action was required at the time.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Telephone Communication to Colonel Herron

subfiles.about: Urgent inquiry regarding instructions to the American Embassy in Tokyo concerning film problems.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Herron informs Mackay that Tokyo representatives sent two urgent cables stating Ambassador Grew had not yet received instructions and was awaiting them to address film quota problems. Herron urges Department assistance due to the critical time element.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Frederick L. Herron to Raymond C. Mackay

subfiles.about: State Department preview and interdepartmental clearance for the sale of an agricultural film to a Japanese professor.
subfiles.from: M. L. Wilson and Breckinridge Long
subfiles.summary: The Department of Agriculture inquired whether the State Department objected to selling a print of 'Block That Termite' to Assistant Professor Saburo Soshiroda of Waseda University. State Department preview officers evaluated the film, rated it excellent, and found no objection to its educational circulation in Japan. Assistant Secretary Breckinridge Long consequently notified Secretary of Agriculture Henry A. Wallace that the Department perceived no objection to the sale.
subfiles.title: Correspondence and Preview Reports Concerning Department of Agriculture Film 'Block That Termite'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording an American traveler's account of cultural filmmaking facilities provided in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note records a conversation with Paul R. Elliott regarding foreign film exhibition. Elliott stated that during his visit to Japan he was afforded every facility and even funds to cover expenses for producing cultural motion pictures.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Motion Pictures Made in Japan (Paul R. Elliott)

subfiles.about: Briefing memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 4733 regarding American film distributor problems and embassy representations.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (J. M. Jones)
subfiles.summary: J. M. Jones summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 4733 concerning restrictions on American moving pictures and profit remittances. He explains that the Embassy avoided intervening on the basis of a questionable private agreement negotiated with Hisaji Kubo, but subsequently approached the Japanese Government to seek clarification of its future import policy.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 4733

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report detailing American film distributor difficulties, Kubo's bribery demands, and Embassy Note No. 1556.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that American distributors had compromised their position by negotiating with Hisaji Kubo, who demanded up to 100,000 yen to bribe the Finance Minister for import permits. Grew declined to intervene on the basis of that dubious private arrangement, but agreed to request clarification of official import policy. The despatch encloses Embassy Note No. 1556 of May 25, 1940, and an attached memorandum outlining past import permits and requesting action on outstanding applications.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 4733: Restrictions on Importations of American Moving Pictures

subfiles.about: Commercial report surveying raw film shortages, regulatory controls, and industry trends in Japan during 1939.
subfiles.from: Donald W. Smith (for Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Assistant Commercial Attaché Donald W. Smith transmits an economic report prepared by Mr. Kaneko of Kodak Japan Ltd.'s Osaka office. The report surveys acute raw stock shortages caused by exchange controls, the enactment of the Motion Picture Law, compulsory screening of cultural films, domestic production statistics, and Japanese motion picture expansion into Manchukuo and North China.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 4862: The Motion Picture Industry in Japan - 1939

subfiles.about: Departmental assessment of Japan's ban on foreign news films and the question of retaliatory measures.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Cabot Coville)
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville reviews Yokohama Despatch No. 708 reporting that Japan would ban foreign news films after October 2, 1940. Addressing Consul Boyce's recommendation to halt imports of Japanese news films into the United States, Coville concludes that American public skepticism would neutralize Japanese propaganda, making retaliatory import prohibitions unnecessary.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Yokohama Despatch No. 708

subfiles.about: Consular report on Japan banning foreign newsreels and exporting war propaganda films to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Consul Boyce reports that Japanese authorities banned foreign news films, including Paramount and Pathé, effective October 2, 1940. He highlights extensive exports of Japanese war propaganda newsreels from Yokohama to the United States and encloses a Japan Times & Mail clipping detailing revised rules mandating officially sanctioned Nippon News Company films.
subfiles.title: Yokohama Despatch No. 708: Importation of American News Films to be Stopped

subfiles.about: Internal exchange on whether to furnish Colonel Herron with a copy of a Tokyo despatch.
subfiles.summary: Francis Colt de Wolf inquires whether there is any objection to transmitting a copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 to Colonel Herron of the Hays organization. The Division of Far Eastern Affairs notes no objection while observing that Herron probably already received the information.
subfiles.title: State Department Routing Slips Regarding Tokyo Despatch on Film Restrictions

subfiles.about: Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 reporting a token Japanese permit allocation for American films.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (J. M. Jones)
subfiles.summary: J. M. Jones outlines the Japanese Foreign Office reply to Ambassador Grew's representations of May 25, 1940. The memorandum notes that Japan granted import permits for only $2,656.72 worth of film prints, a negligible fraction of normal commercial requirements.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5123

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report transmitting Foreign Minister Matsuoka's note granting token film import permits.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an English translation of a note dated October 7, 1940, from Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka replying to Embassy representations of May 25. Matsuoka states that the Ministry of Finance granted permission on September 24 for American motion picture imports not exceeding $2,656.72 in print cost.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5123: Japanese Reply to American Representations

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's note to the MPPDA.
subfiles.summary: Thomas Burke transmits to Colonel Frederick L. Herron a copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 and the enclosed Foreign Office note concerning Japanese restrictions on American motion picture imports.
subfiles.title: Letter from Thomas Burke to Colonel Frederick L. Herron

subfiles.about: Summary of Yokohama Despatch No. 723 detailing Japanese propaganda newsreel shipments to California.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Herbert T. Fales)
subfiles.summary: Herbert T. Fales summarizes Yokohama Despatch No. 723, noting that Japanese propaganda newsreels shipped to the Japanese Theater Association in Los Angeles featured the Emperor's activities, celebrations of the Tripartite Pact, and the East Asia Recreation Congress.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Yokohama Despatch No. 723

subfiles.about: Consular report transmitting synopses of Japanese propaganda newsreels shipped to Los Angeles on the M.S. Tatuta Maru.
subfiles.summary: Consul Boyce reports on ongoing exports of Japanese propaganda films to the United States, enclosing resumes of newsreels shipped by Nichibei Kogyo Kaisha of Yokohama to the Japanese Theatre Association of Los Angeles on the M.S. Tatuta Maru. The synopses detail items from Nippon News Nos. 19 and 20 and Asahi Home Graph No. 52 depicting Imperial visits, fleet reviews, Axis alliance celebrations, and wartime events.
subfiles.title: Yokohama Despatch No. 723: Japanese Propaganda

subfiles.about: Acknowledgement of receipt of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 regarding Japanese film restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Herron thanks Thomas Burke for sending a copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 5123 regarding restrictions on the importation of American motion pictures into Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Thomas Burke

subfiles.about: Urgent recommendation from Tokyo film representatives urging State Department pressure on National City Bank.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a telegram from the American Motion Picture Association of Japan ('Ampica') to the Motion Picture Producers Association in New York. The association recommends contacting the State Department to urge National City Bank to retain their cash deposits, warning that Japanese national bonds are a dangerous investment.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1369 (Transmitting Message from Ampica)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report on National City Bank demanding withdrawal of 8,000,000 yen in American film company deposits.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that National City Bank requested American film companies to withdraw about 8,000,000 yen in cash deposits, proposing they redeposit the funds with the Bank of Japan or buy Japanese national bonds yielding 3.5% remittable interest. Embassy officers advised company representatives that the US Government disapproved of investing funds in Japanese government bonds and urged them to contact their New York home offices.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 1370 on National City Bank Deposit Crisis

subfiles.about: Departmental transmittal of Tokyo Embassy message regarding National City Bank deposits and Japanese bonds.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton relays to Colonel Herron the cable from American film representatives in Tokyo advising against purchasing risky Japanese national bonds and seeking pressure on National City Bank. Hamilton notes that the situation is unclear to the Department and invites Herron to provide background information.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Colonel Frederick L. Herron

subfiles.about: Industry explanation that blocked bank deposits in Tokyo would be managed individually rather than collectively.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Herron replies that foreign managers discussed the Tokyo message and decided that handling frozen bank funds was an individual corporate matter rather than a group action. He explains that several companies did not bank with National City Bank and preferred to resolve the issue independently.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Departmental memo proposing to reiterate US objections to Paramount investing in Japanese bonds.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Tokyo Telegram No. 148 reporting that Paramount's Tokyo office was instructed to invest in Japanese national bonds. Fearing this precedent would force other firms to comply, officers recommend contacting Colonel Herron or Paramount executives Adolph Zukor and Barney Balaban to emphasize the Department's opposition.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Paramount's Purchase of Japanese Bonds

subfiles.about: Diplomatic warning that Paramount Tokyo was instructed to buy Japanese bonds, setting a dangerous precedent.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Paramount is the only American film firm in Tokyo instructed to invest in Japanese national bonds. Grew warns that if Paramount proceeds, added pressure will fall on other American firms with frozen funds, and suggests the Department reiterate its policy to Paramount.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 148 Regarding Paramount's Bond Purchase Instructions

subfiles.about: Transmission of emergency query from Warner Brothers' Tokyo manager Shathin to New York executive Hummel.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits an urgent cable from Warner Brothers' Tokyo manager Shathin to Hummel in New York. In view of the worsening crisis, Shathin asks for definite instructions regarding company affairs, staff, and personal safety in the event of an emergency.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 152 (Transmitting Message for Hummel, Warner Brothers)

subfiles.about: Departmental letter transmitting Tokyo Embassy cable containing Shathin's emergency inquiry to Warner Brothers.
subfiles.summary: Nathaniel P. Davis transmits to Warner Brothers in New York a copy of Tokyo Telegram No. 152 containing Shathin's inquiry for Hummel regarding emergency procedures.
subfiles.title: Letter from Nathaniel P. Davis to Warner Brothers

subfiles.about: Industry response regarding individual company autonomy and Paramount's reported bond purchase.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Herron replies to Hamilton's letter of February 13, stating that foreign managers had agreed each company must handle investments individually. He doubts Paramount invested heavily and assumes it did so only under irresistible Japanese pressure, adding that he is relaying the Department's position to member companies.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick L. Herron to Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Departmental request to Colonel Herron to dissuade Paramount from investing in Japanese national bonds.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton writes to Colonel Herron noting Ambassador Grew's report that Paramount instructed its Tokyo manager to invest in Japanese national bonds. Emphasizing that bond purchases by one firm increase pressure on others, Hamilton asks Herron to bring the Department's disapproval to Paramount's attention.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Colonel Frederick L. Herron

subfiles.about: Confidential transmittal to Ambassador Grew of Department correspondence with Colonel Herron on bond purchases.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Grew confidential copies of Hamilton's letter of February 13 to Colonel Herron and Herron's reply of February 14 regarding Paramount's investments in Japanese national bonds.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 2127 to the American Ambassador at Tokyo

subfiles.about: Acknowledgement of Department letter regarding Paramount's bond investments.
subfiles.summary: Carl E. Milliken, Secretary of the MPPDA, acknowledges receipt of Hamilton's letter of March 17 concerning Paramount Tokyo's bond purchase instructions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Carl E. Milliken to Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Warner Brothers request for telegraphic transmission of Hummel's reply to Tokyo manager Shathin.
subfiles.summary: Karl G. Macdonald requests the State Department to cable a message via the Tokyo Embassy from Hummel to Shathin. The message states that Hummel does not understand Shathin's earlier cable and requests clarification before providing emergency instructions.
subfiles.title: Letter from Karl G. Macdonald to Secretary of State (Attn: Nathaniel P. Davis)

subfiles.about: Departmental confirmation of telegraphic transmission of Hummel's cable to Tokyo manager Shathin.
subfiles.summary: Nathaniel P. Davis informs Warner Brothers that Hummel's message for Shathin has been telegraphed to the American Embassy in Tokyo for delivery.
subfiles.title: Letter from Nathaniel P. Davis to Warner Brothers Pictures, Inc.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report that Paramount's Tokyo manager placed an order for Japanese Government bonds.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Paramount's Tokyo representative informed him that he placed a purchase order on March 6 for an undisclosed amount of Japanese Government bonds.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 371 on Paramount Bond Order

subfiles.about: Departmental expression of regret over Paramount's purchase order for Japanese Government bonds.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton informs Colonel Herron that Paramount's representative in Tokyo placed an order on March 6 for Japanese Government bonds. Hamilton expresses the Department's regret and reaffirms its policy opposing American investments in Japanese national bonds.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Colonel Frederick L. Herron

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Paramount executive John W. Hicks Jr.'s letter explaining bond transactions and questioning US policy.
subfiles.summary: Carl E. Milliken forwards a letter from John W. Hicks, Jr., Vice President of Paramount Pictures. Hicks sets forth the chronology of the bond purchases, explaining that the transaction allowed dollar remittances of 3.5% interest and an easement on blocked funds. Hicks confirms that further purchases were cancelled immediately upon learning of State Department disapproval, but questions why the Department opposes a policy that retrieves American dollars and depletes Japanese reserves.
subfiles.title: Letter from Carl E. Milliken to Maxwell M. Hamilton Transmitting Letter from John W. Hicks, Jr.
